items.title: You are paralysed multiple times every night
items.claim: During REM sleep, when most dreams occur, motor neurons to your skeletal muscles are actively inhibited. You cannot move. This is REM atonia — and when it fails, people act out their dreams.
items.prompt: Why does the brain paralyse you while dreaming?

options.text: To prevent acting out dream content — the same brain regions that command movement are active in REM as in waking, but spinal motor neurons are blocked from receiving the signals
To stop heart rate from rising

items.reveal_title: REM behavior disorder and Schenck's discovery
items.reveal:
The brainstem (specifically the pons and medulla) sends inhibitory signals to spinal motor neurons during REM. The motor cortex fires in patterns resembling waking; the descending commands reach the spinal cord but cannot trigger muscle contraction.

In REM Behavior Disorder (Schenck 1986), this paralysis fails. Patients punch, kick, vocalise and act out vivid dreams. RBD is strongly associated with later Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia — the brainstem regions controlling REM atonia degrade early in these conditions.

Narcolepsy with cataplexy is the opposite failure: REM-style atonia intrudes into waking life, triggered by emotion. Modafinil and other treatments stabilise the boundary between sleep states.
items.why: Sleep is imagined as 'off'. REM sleep is intensely active — and the body needs active suppression to prevent the brain's instructions reaching the muscles.

items.title: Sprinting and marathon running use chemically different fuels
items.claim: Aerobic respiration of one glucose produces about 30-32 ATP. Anaerobic glycolysis produces only 2 ATP. Yet sprinters rely on the anaerobic path. Why use a pathway that wastes 94% of glucose's chemical energy?

options.text: It's faster — sprint muscle can produce ATP via glycolysis ~100x faster per second than oxidative phosphorylation can. Power output wins over efficiency in short bursts

items.reveal:
Aerobic respiration is the efficient long path: glycolysis (cytoplasm) -> pyruvate -> Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix) -> oxidative phosphorylation -> ~30-32 ATP per glucose, with CO2 and water as byproducts.

Anaerobic glycolysis stops at pyruvate, converts it to lactate (regenerating the NAD+ glycolysis needs), and quits. Yield: 2 ATP per glucose. But it runs without oxygen and at ~100x the rate of mitochondrial ATP synthesis.

Sprint events (100m, weightlifting): mostly anaerobic. Lactate builds up. Burns. The 'oxygen debt' you owe after sprinting is the cost of clearing the lactate and replenishing phosphocreatine.

Endurance events (marathon, cycling): mostly aerobic, fuelled by glucose at first, then fat. Fat yields ~106 ATP per palmitate molecule but is metabolised slowly — fine for steady output.

Yeasts do alcoholic fermentation (pyruvate -> ethanol + CO2) instead of lactate fermentation. Same logic: regenerate NAD+ and keep glycolysis running when oxygen runs low.
items.why: Efficiency seems obviously best. For peak power, throughput beats efficiency every time — which is why sprinters look chemically different from marathoners during a race.

items.title: You synthesise your body weight in ATP every day
items.claim: ATP is the cell's energy currency. Your body contains only about 50 grams at any moment, but you turn it over so fast that you make and consume the equivalent of your full body mass — 60 to 80 kilograms — daily.
items.prompt: How can a tiny pool turn over so much?

options.text: Each ATP molecule is hydrolysed and re-synthesised hundreds of times per day; mitochondria continuously rebuild ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using the proton motive force from respiration
Most of the body's mass is ATP
ATP is consumed only during exercise

items.reveal:
An adult at rest uses about 2000 kcal per day. Each ATP hydrolysis releases ~7.3 kcal/mol of free energy under standard conditions, more under cellular conditions.

Working through: ~65 kg of ATP cycled per day, give or take. Each molecule of ATP cycles roughly 1000-1500 times daily.

The cell stores essentially no ATP for emergencies. It maintains a flux instead. Stop respiration and your ATP pool depletes in seconds — which is exactly why cyanide is so fast.

Muscles store some quick-access energy as phosphocreatine (a few seconds of all-out sprint) and glycogen (~minutes), but ATP itself is continuously regenerated, not stockpiled.

This is metabolism's deep design choice: a small, dynamic currency pool, refilled by continuous oxidation of food.
items.why: Energy storage feels like the obvious solution. Cells went the other way — keep almost no ATP, rebuild it constantly. The flux IS the metabolism.
